newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: East Asia ready for more active bond market.
newsitem.headline: East Asia ready for more active bond market.

text.p: East Asia is ready for a more developed bond market to raise the large sums needed for infrastructure improvements, but some hurdles to its establishment must be cleared, economists and bankers say.
The bond market in East Asia is expected to grow rapidly in the coming years, participants at a business forum connected to the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) said on Saturday.
The market's development would answer the need for long-term and cheaper capital to finance the large infrastructure requirements of the growing Asian economies.
"Although progress has been made, there are some weaknesses in East Asian markets," said Francis Colaco, a World Bank senior adviser.
The East Asia region includes China, Hong Kong, South Korea, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan and Thailand, which are all part of the 18 member-economies of APEC.

Colaco cited the need for the expansion of the number of credible rating agencies in the region, the timely disclosure and reliability of information released, the credibity of accounting and auditing procedures, and the legal protection of bondholders.
The establishment of a regulatory system is also required to ensure investor safety and promote market development, participants said.
Lower taxes and a mechanism to spur an active secondary market for bonds would also have to be addressed, they said.

According to the World Bank, East Asian economies have raised in the international bond markets a total of $14.2 billion in the first half of 1996, $21.6 billion in the entire 1995, and $19.2 billion in 1994.
"The region now has the necessary conditions for the emergence of more active bond markets," said Paul Dickie, director for infrastructure, energy and financial sectors of the Asian Development Bank.
He cited the strong economic growth potential, rising creditworthiness and ample supply of potential issuers.

Jeffrey Koo, chairman of the Taiwan-based China Trust Commercial Bank, said APEC members need to establish a unified bond rating system, a bond settlement system and a cooperative credit checking mechanism.
Participants at the forum also cited the importance of opening up financial sectors in some Asian countries in order to sustain the growth of their economy.
"Especially in the areas of banking, securities, insurance and peripheral financial services, most Asian countries still exercise fairly rigid controls, " said Koo.
"In Asia, Hong Kong offers the best attraction for investment by providing the most liberalised economy and financial system," he said.

"The Philippines, Malaysia and Thailand are also good examples of a government created to attract capital. In addition, Taiwan is making efforts to become a regional operation and financial center," he added.

Savings in the East Asia region have averaged over 30 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), which would make available more capital for infrastucture requirements which are expected to increase to seven percent of GDP in the next 10 to 15 years from the current five percent, Dickie said.
